newsitem.title: GERMANY: Feature - Berlin shopping street has glitz but few buyers.
newsitem.headline: Feature - Berlin shopping street has glitz but few buyers.

text.p: They dreamed of restoring the elegance to one of Berlin's most famous shopping streets, but a year after the opening of its flagship department store, investors are getting cold feet and much of it still looks like a ghost town.

A champagne gala feted the opening of luxury French store Galeries Lafayette on Friedrichstrasse, which opened to the public in March last year, and Berlin's Mayor Eberhard Diepgen hailed it as a boost to the street in impoverished east Berlin.

But dire unemployment figures, which have hovered at around 20 percent in eastern Germany since the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, have cast a long shadow over the luxury mile reconstructed to match the glamour of any European metropolis.

"The people look and stare, but not everyone buys something," lamented Claude Fabre, CEO of Galeries Lafayette, in a newspaper interview before he was replaced by French executive Joseph Stoffer in September.
Despite management reshuffles, a token strike, poor sales and the fact that it has a few more years to go before the government moves to the capital in 1999, his successor was more optimistic.
"The first year was difficult, but the sales we wanted did materialise," Stoffer told Reuters. "We learned a lot."
"Everybody says we're going to close, but I tell them, maybe in 200 years. We're there and we're staying there."
THE EAST-WEST DIVIDE ON FRIEDRICHSTRASSE

More than 3.0 billion marks ($1.8 billion) have been put into the three-km (two-mile) street, the most developed area in Berlin after Europe's largest construction site on Potsdamer Platz and the future government area near the Reichstag parliament building.

While prosperous west Germans complain of a dearth of luxury flats, world-class office buildings and chic shopping in Berlin, they often say the development boom in the east lacks the elan of more traditional west Berlin shopping institutions.

At the same time, the developments on Friedrichstrasse have struck many easterners as too opulent, impractical and more suited to sophisticated cities like Stuttgart or Munich than to Berlin, with its budget crises and no-frills sense of fashion.

"It bears no resemblance to the Friedrichstrasse from before the war," said Liselotta Gaury, 80, who was window-shopping with a friend. "There used to be so many little candy shops, (selling) things that people could afford."

"We keep asking ourselves, 'Who could shop here now?'" said Gaury, a native west Berliner. Many people from east Berlin just shrug as they walk by tempting wares, unsurprised that the city's growth seems to be passing them by.
"I find the prices appropriate for the new Berlin, with the exception of Galeries Lafayette, which is outrageous," said Bernard Barte, 70, from east Berlin.
"But it's a shame that the architecture is so cold, so boxy, so unimaginative and so flat," Barte added, inspecting the street's modern glass facades.

At the corner of the historic Unter den Linden, communist East Berlin's main boulevard, lies the Lindencorso, a 30,000 sq metre (322,000 square foot) complex of office space, shops and flats -- only 10 percent of which has been pre-leased.

Further south down the Friedrichstrasse, there is a new chic indoor mall, the Friedrichstadt Passagen, including American franchise restaurant Planet Hollywood and designer shops Gucci and Donna Karan due to open this spring.

Yet despite its attractive glass and marble design, in part contributed by star architect I.M. Pei's firm, the Passagen's 8,200 square metres (88,000 square feet) remain only 45 percent leased and only 20 percent of its office space is occupied.

Avant-garde art galleries, pricy antique shops and adventurous fashion designers have been granted free short-term leases to fill the empty floor space and create an atmosphere of activity in the Passagen until paying tenants can be found.

The former communist East German government had planned a western-style shopping plaza on the site of the Passagen in the 1980s. It was nearly completed when western investors arrived after unification and promptly demolished it.

Checkpoint Charlie, the Allied border crossing that divided Friedrichstrasse between East and West and was immortalised in countless spy thrillers, is being replaced for the century's end by a retail and office development of the same name.

A spokeswoman for the Checkpoint Charlie development, formerly known as the American Business Center, said the five-building complex still under construction had just started opening its doors to potential leaseholders.
THE FAIRY TALE OF FRIEDRICHSTRASSE
Some say the idea that the street was ever a chic European crossroads is more the invention of today's investors and that the revival of its "glorious past" may be just a pipe dream.

The street was named after the Prussian King Friedrich III, who intended it as the main thoroughfare of his capital, but it soon became better known for its seedy dance halls, cheap markets and, in 1900, about 10,000 prostitutes.

The Kurfuerstendamm avenue has served as the city's seat of wealth and elegance since the turn of the century and the planners on Friedrichstrasse have hoped to capture some of its glamour, and eventually eclipse it as a Berlin institution.
Yet Friedrichstrasse has helped to recreate a street life that east Berlin had lacked for decades.

Street musicians and summer street fairs there last year drew families to peer at the budding architectural spectacles, replacing the often eerie stillness that reigned before the Berlin Wall came down. ($ = 1.705 German Marks)
